:::{#exm-perfect-secrecy}
#### The one-time pad with a two-bit message

<!-- no-figure: the example is two numbers -->

Let the message take the four values $0, 1, 2, 3$ (two [bits](entropy.qmd#def-bit)) with [probabilities](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/probability-basics.html#def-probability) $0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1$.
The key is uniform on the same four values,
and the ciphertext is the bitwise exclusive or of message and key.
The R chunk below builds the [joint distribution](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/random-variables.html#def-joint-distribution) of message and ciphertext,
and computes the [mutual information](entropy.qmd#def-mutual-information) between them.

```{r}
#| label: perfect-secrecy
prior <- c(0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1)
joint <- matrix(0, nrow = 4, ncol = 4)
for (m in 0:3) {
  for (k in 0:3) {
    c_value <- bitwXor(m, k)
    joint[m + 1, c_value + 1] <- joint[m + 1, c_value + 1] + prior[m + 1] / 4
  }
}
cipher_prob <- colSums(joint)
product <- outer(prior, cipher_prob)
max_gap <- max(abs(joint - product))
mutual_info <- sum(joint * log2(joint / product))
c(max_gap = max_gap, mutual_info = mutual_info)
```

The ciphertext is uniform, with probability $`r cipher_prob[1]`$ on each value,
and the largest gap between the joint distribution and the product of the two [marginal distributions](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/random-variables.html#def-marginal) is $`r max_gap`$.
So the mutual information is $`r round(mutual_info, 10)`$ bits:
the pad has [perfect secrecy](#def-perfect-secrecy) for these message probabilities.

:::
